summary.text: DNA is a molecule made of two long chains that coil around each other into a double helix.
It carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses.
Those instructions are written in the order of four bases along each chain, and the information is copied when the two strands separate.

facts.label: Shape
facts.value: Two strands coiled into a double helix

facts.label: Pairing rule
facts.value: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G

facts.label: Strand direction
facts.value: The two strands run in opposite directions

items.prompt: One strand of a DNA double helix reads A-T-T-C-G. Looking straight across, which bases sit on the partner strand, in matching positions?

options.label: A-T-T-C-G
G-C-T-T-A
C-G-G-A-T
T-A-A-G-C

items.explain: Bases pair by fixed rules: A with T and C with G, so each base is matched with its partner.

items.prompt: A cell is about to divide and its DNA strands pull apart. What makes it possible to copy the information at this point?

options.label: Each strand holds half the information, and the cell discards the rest
Both strands store the same biological information
The strands are rebuilt from scratch from proteins
Only one strand carries instructions; the other is a spare

items.explain: Both strands of double-stranded DNA store the same information, and it is replicated when the two strands separate.

items.prompt: A scientist wants to find the DNA inside a bacterium. Where should she look?

options.label: Inside a nucleus, packed into long chromosomes
Inside mitochondria only
In the cytoplasm, in circular chromosomes
Outside the cell, floating freely

items.explain: Bacteria and other prokaryotes store their DNA only in the cytoplasm, in circular chromosomes, while eukaryotes keep most of theirs in the nucleus.

items.prompt: A lab examines a nucleic acid strand and finds uracil in the spot where thymine would normally be. How was this strand most likely made?

options.label: Copied from a DNA strand by transcription
Duplicated as part of chromosome replication
Built directly out of amino acids
Coiled up by histone proteins

items.explain: In transcription, RNA is made using a DNA strand as a template, and RNA substitutes uracil for thymine.

items.prompt: Two cars drive on a road, one in each lane, heading different ways. In a DNA double helix, how do the two strands compare in direction?

options.label: Both point the same way, like cars in one lane
One direction changes randomly along the helix
Direction is meaningless for the strands
They are antiparallel, each running against the other

items.explain: Each strand has a direction, and in the double helix the direction of one strand is opposite to the other, so they are antiparallel.

items.prompt: In eukaryotic cells, what do chromatin proteins such as histones do for DNA?

options.label: Pack it tightly and help control which parts are transcribed
Supply the four bases that make up the code
Turn it into protein directly by translation
Join its sugars together into a backbone

items.explain: Histones and other chromatin proteins compact and organize DNA, and these structures help control which parts of it are transcribed.

paragraphs.heading: A molecule that holds instructions
paragraphs.text: DNA, short for deoxyribonucleic acid, is a long molecule built from two chains wound around each other in a double helix. It holds the genetic instructions that every known living thing, and many viruses, use to develop, work, grow and reproduce. DNA belongs to a family of molecules called nucleic acids, along with its cousin RNA. Nucleic acids rank with proteins, lipids and complex carbohydrates as one of the four big classes of large molecules that all known life depends on.

paragraphs.heading: Beads on a chain
paragraphs.text: Each of the two chains is a polymer, a long molecule made by linking many small repeating units. In DNA those units are nucleotides, so each chain is called a polynucleotide. A nucleotide has three parts: a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and one of four bases containing nitrogen. The four bases are cytosine, guanine, adenine and thymine, written C, G, A and T.

paragraphs.heading: The backbone and its direction
paragraphs.text: Covalent bonds join the sugar of one nucleotide to the phosphate of the next, so sugar and phosphate alternate down the length of the chain. This alternating strip is called the backbone, and one base is attached to each sugar. The way the sugars' carbon atoms line up along the backbone gives each strand a direction. The two strands of the helix point in opposite directions, which is why they are described as antiparallel.

paragraphs.heading: How the two strands pair
paragraphs.text: The bases on one strand bond to the bases on the other through hydrogen bonds, following a strict rule: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The bases fall into two families, the single-ringed pyrimidines (thymine and cytosine) and the double-ringed purines (adenine and guanine). Both strands of the pair store the same information. When the strands come apart, that information can be copied.

paragraphs.heading: Writing the message
paragraphs.text: The genetic information lies in the order of the four bases along the backbone, much as meaning lies in the order of letters in a word. Strands of RNA are built using a DNA strand as a template, a step called transcription. RNA uses the same base partners except that uracil, U, takes the place of thymine. Through the genetic code, these RNA strands then set the order of amino acids in a protein, a step called translation.

paragraphs.heading: Where cells keep their DNA
paragraphs.text: Animals, plants, fungi and protists, the eukaryotes, keep most of their DNA in the cell nucleus, with some in mitochondria or chloroplasts. Their DNA is packed into long structures called chromosomes. Proteins such as histones pack and organize it, and this packing helps control which parts of the DNA are transcribed. Bacteria and archaea, the prokaryotes, instead keep their DNA only in the cytoplasm, in circular chromosomes.

paragraphs.heading: Copying before division
paragraphs.text: Before a cell divides, its chromosomes are copied in a process called DNA replication. That way each new daughter cell receives a complete set. In the common form of DNA, called B-DNA, the helix twists to the right, like an ordinary screw that moves forward when you turn it clockwise.
